newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean aid to arrive in North this month and next.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean aid to arrive in North this month and next.

text.p: The $10 million in food aid that South Korea has pledged to famine-threatened North Korea will arrive this month and next month, Seoul's Unification Ministry said on Friday.

The 50,000 tonnes of corn and 300 tonnes of powdered milk are part of $16 million worth of aid Seoul has pledged in response to a $95.5 million appeal by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) to stave off famine in the North.
Corn/soybean blend worth $6 million has already been sent to the North.

South Korea's Agriculture Ministry will invite tenders to buy 50,000 tonnes of foreign corn for shipment to the North Korean port of Nampo, near Pyongyang, by the end of August, a ministry statement said.
The powdered milk will be bought in South Korea and delivered this month, it added.
After consulting with the WFP, the Seoul government has decided to provide relief supplies directly to the North instead of donating money to the Rome-based U.N. agency.
On Thursday, the U.S. State Department said the last of $25 million worth of American food aid was about to arrive in the hard-hit northeastern area of the communist state.
The WFP said on Tuesday it had received almost all of the $95.5 million it had requested in its latest appeal to help ease hunger in North Korea.
U.N. officials have said North Korea, hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, still needs more food aid.

The United States and South Korea have said they will consider any further appeals by the WFP, although large-scale assistance would have to wait until Pyongyang comes to the table for peace talks aimed at closing the book on the 1950-53 Korean War.

Pyongyang has agreed to an August 5 meeting in New York of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to arrange four-nation talks on a peace treaty to replace the truce agreement that ended the fighting in the Korean conflict but, technically, not the war itself.
